1:
Why Paul signs his letters when earlier writers did not Chrysostom answers from circumstance. Moses wrote five books and nowhere put his name to them, nor did those who continued the history after him, nor Matthew, John, Mark or Luke; but Paul everywhere sets his own name. The reason is that they wrote to people present, so it had been superfluous to show themselves, while Paul sent his writings from afar in the form of a letter, for which cause the name was necessary. And if in Hebrews he omits it, that too is after his own wise judgment: they felt prejudiced against him, and lest on hearing the name at the outset they should stop up all admission to his discourse, he subtly won their attention by concealing it. Theodoret answers from character instead: governors and generals superscribe their letters with their dignities, puffed up by each fresh tide of honour, whereas this apostle is content to call himself one born out of due time and the chief of sinners.

Yet Theodoret grants he prefixes the appellations grace had obtained him, so that those receiving his epistles, seeing the writer's honours, might the more readily welcome them. Where the name itself came from they divide. Theodoret says he begins by Paul not as named of old by his parents but as preferred to it after his call, as Simon to Peter, the sons of Zebedee to Sons of Thunder, Jacob to Israel and Abram to Abraham. Gill canvasses the proposals and prefers another: some think the name changed at his conversion, others at that of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, others that he was so called from the littleness of his stature, but rather he had two names, as was usual with the Jews, one used among the Gentiles and one at home. Calvin rules out the proconsul, since Luke shows he was so called before that time.

Servant Ellicott would render more strictly slave, yet holds the received word not wrong, since the compulsory and degrading side of service is not put forward and the modern idea of slavery carries altogether different associations. Robertson calls it bond-slave, opening an epistle here for the first time. Henry takes it for a title of honour which Paul glories in, not as the Jewish teachers with their Rabbi, Rabbi, but a servant, a steward in the house; and observes that Paul builds his authority on his call, not running without sending as the false apostles did. Wesley puts the calling in a sentence, that while God calls he makes what he calls, and adds that since the Judaizing teachers disputed his claim it is with great propriety that he asserts it at the very entrance of an epistle wherein their principles are entirely overthrown. Gill lists what he is not a servant of: not of sin, nor Satan, nor man, nor Moses and his law, nor the traditions of the elders.

Separated Henry turns on the Pharisees, whose very name came from separation, since they separated themselves to the study of the law. Ellicott distinguishes two separations: the reference here is to the historical selection, as when the leaders at Antioch were told to separate Barnabas and Saul, human instruments carrying out the divine will, whereas in Galatians it is the more distant act of divine predestination; and the ambiguous genitive of the gospel of God seems to mean the gospel which proceeds from God. Wesley makes it successive, from the bulk of other men, from other Jews, from other disciples. Barnes calls the epistle what it has usually been regarded, the most difficult portion of the New Testament; Clarke refers its authorship to Paley's Horae Paulinae, which he says satisfies the most fastidious scepticism; Robertson notes that the oldest manuscripts title it simply, To the Romans, and that it stands first as the most important of Paul's epistles.
2:
That the gospel was promised beforehand Calvin treats as an argument with three steps. Since the suspicion of being new subtracts much from a doctrine's authority, Paul confirms the faith of the gospel by antiquity, as though he said that Christ came not unexpectedly, nor introduced a doctrine of a new kind and not heard of before, since he and his gospel had been promised from the beginning of the world; but because antiquity is often fabulous, he brings approved witnesses, the prophets of God, to remove every suspicion; and thirdly adds that their testimonies were duly recorded, in the Holy Scriptures. Gill puts it plainly, that the gospel is commended from its antiquity, being no novel doctrine or upstart notion but what God had conceived in his own breast from eternity. Wesley compresses it into three words, of old time, frequently, solemnly, adding that promise and accomplishment confirm each other.

Why the scriptures are called holy without an article three of them notice, and none for the same reason. Ellicott finds a nicety of meaning in the omission, which throws a slight stress on the epithet: not merely certain books which go by the name of holy scriptures, but certain writings the character of which is holy, holy as containing these very promises. Robertson observes that the phrase has no article yet is definite, follows Sanday and Headlam in calling it perhaps the earliest such use, and concludes that Paul definitely finds God's gospel in the Holy Scriptures. Theodoret makes it a statement about the canon: he does not call them holy for no reason, but firstly to show that he acknowledged their inspiration, and secondly as excluding all other writings, since the inspired book alone contains all we can need. Clarke keeps to the substance, that in law and prophets alike God showed his purpose to bring in a more perfect and glorious state of things.

That the subject of the gospel is the Son they state in the strongest terms available to them. Calvin calls it a remarkable passage teaching that the whole gospel is included in Christ, so that whoever removes one step from him withdraws from the gospel; since he is the living and express image of the Father, no wonder he alone is set before us as one to whom our whole faith is directed and in whom it centres, so that this is a definition of the gospel. Barnes says the same negatively, that there is no good news to man respecting salvation except what comes by Jesus Christ, and this is the whole of it. Gill makes Christ as Son of God, Saviour of sinners and only Mediator the sum and substance of the Gospel; Clarke widens the content to the conception, birth, preaching, miracles, passion, death, resurrection and ascension.

The word rendered was made Barnes will not leave at its usual sense. It commonly means to be or to become, but is used of being born, as when God sent forth his Son made of a woman, and in the saying that before Abraham was, I am; and in that sense it seems used here. Robertson finds the deity of Christ stated here and the real humanity set alongside it by the phrase according to the flesh. Wesley notices the order rather than the fact: both natures are mentioned, the human first, because the divine was not manifested in full evidence till after the resurrection. Theodoret keeps both in one clause, the Son begotten of the Father before all eternity yet making himself of David's seed; Gill distinguishes relation from names, the Son being of the same nature with the Father, equal to him and distinct from him, while Jesus signifies a Saviour and Christ anointed.
4:
The word rendered declared Calvin reports as an old division. Some of the ancients, he says, gave the verb the sense of proved, demonstrated or exhibited; but others hold that it has not this meaning in the New Testament, and means limited, determined, decreed, constituted. Either sense, he judges, would amount to the same thing, namely that Christ was visibly determined or constituted the Son of God. Barnes canvasses the versions and finds them just as divided, the Syriac reading that he was known to be the Son of God, the Vulgate that he was predestinated the Son of God, the Arabic that he was destined by power; and he gives the root sense as to bound or fix limits, as to a field. Clarke traces the same root to our own word horizon, the line that determines the farthest visible part of the earth, and takes the sense here as an exhibition so complete as to render the matter indubitable.

What was declared, and when, they are careful to distinguish. Gill insists the word is not made, as in the verse before: Christ did not begin to be the Son of God when he was made of the seed of David, but he who existed as such from everlasting was manifested in the flesh, and it is this divine sonship that is declared. Robertson says the same and dates the declaration, that he was the Son of God in his preincarnate state and still so after the Incarnation, but the resurrection of the dead definitely marked him off as God's Son, because of his claims about himself and his prophecy that he would rise on the third day. Wesley makes the resurrection both the fountain and the object of our faith; and Clarke calls it a manifest proof at once of our Lord's innocence, of the truth of his doctrine, and of the fulfilment of all that the prophets had spoken.

The spirit of holiness Ellicott examines and declines to settle. It stands in antithesis to according to the flesh, and so comes where we should expect the words, in his divine nature; yet there is a difference, the precise shade of which is not easy to define. Are we to regard the phrase as simply convertible with Holy Spirit? Not quite. Are we to look on it as corresponding to the flesh, as spirit and flesh correspond in man? Again not quite, or not merely, since the spirit of Christ is human, Christ having taken our nature upon him. Wesley makes exactly the identification Ellicott refuses, glossing the phrase in three words as his divine nature; Theodoret simply recites the clause whole, declaring the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead.

Whether grace and apostleship are one thing or two Gill states as an open alternative, either one and the same, the favour and honour of being Christ's apostles, or different things, the one in order to the other. Clarke thinks them probably one, the phrase meaning the grace of the apostleship, that is, the apostolical office, and cites other Pauline uses of the word. Calvin names the figure outright, that by mentioning grace and apostleship apart Paul adopts a hypallage, a grammatical figure by which a noun is put in a case different from the one it ought to have, so that the sense is gratuitous apostleship, or the favour of the apostleship, wholly through divine favour and not through his own worth. Ellicott keeps them distinct and quotes Augustine's ground for doing so, that grace is common to the Apostle with all believers while the apostleship is his own. Of the plural, Barnes says it is probably put for the singular, and Ellicott that Paul means himself alone but uses it with delicate tact, to avoid the appearance of egotism.
6:
Whether the letter said in Rome at all is disputed. Ellicott observes that one manuscript of some importance, the Codex Boernerianus, omits the words, and with some others alters beloved of God to in the love of God, so substituting for the special address to the Romans a general one to all who are in the love of God; it omits at Rome again in the fifteenth verse, and traces of the reading appear in Origen and the Ambrosian Hilary. These peculiarities, he says, support the theory that the epistle circulated, with the Apostle's own sanction, as a general treatise with the personal matter eliminated. Robertson concedes the facts and refuses the conclusion: one late uncial of the tenth century and a cursive, evidence late and slight, which by no means shows this was so in the first century, and not comparable with the absence of in Ephesus from the two best manuscripts of the Ephesian letter.

Gill takes the address at its widest: the inscription is not to the Roman emperor, nor the senate, nor all the inhabitants, but to all the saints there, rich or poor, bond or free, Jew or Gentile, all one in Christ Jesus. Called of Jesus Christ Ellicott renders not called by Jesus Christ but called and so belonging to him. Robertson takes the genitive as predicate, though allowing the ablative, called of or from Jesus Christ. What calling itself imports divides them. Barnes says the word denotes not merely an external invitation but the internal or effectual call which secures conformity to the will of him who calls, and is thus synonymous with believers. Clarke takes the plainer sense: to be called by the Gospel is to be invited to believe; he allows only that the word sometimes means constituted, as in the first verse. Of saints Barnes gives the radical idea as what is separated from a common to a sacred use, answering to the Hebrew word used of the temple and the priests.

Ellicott adds that the epithets, from a modern writer applied to a modern church, would seem indiscriminating or conventional; they correspond to no actual condition of things but to the ideal condition in which all Christians are supposed to be, held up as a mirror to convict them if they are unfaithful. Grace and peace both Barnes and Clarke treat at lexicon length, Clarke distinguishing twelve senses of the one and nine of the other, and deriving peace from a verb meaning to bind. Ellicott is briefer: the two nearly answer to two ordinary forms of Jewish salutation, grace being the state of favour into which the Christian is admitted and peace the state of mind resulting from it. Calvin, quoting Turrettin, sets the greeting against the health and joy the ancient Greeks and Romans wished each other, and declines to narrow peace to quietness of conscience, since Paul meant a summary of all God's blessings.

Calvin finds the order instructive: first the Lord made us the objects of his love, then he called us, and thirdly he called us to holiness, so that Paul by no means ascribes the praise of our salvation to ourselves. That grace and peace are asked of Christ as of the Father none of them passes over. Barnes builds on it, that no man would introduce Christ's name in such a connection who did not believe him equal with God; Robertson quotes Sanday and Headlam, that Paul, if not formally enunciating a doctrine of the Divinity of Christ, held a view which cannot really be distinguished from it; Wesley says it is one and the same peace and one and the same grace which is from God and from Jesus Christ. Theodoret, on the verse before, hears Paul disclaim any trespass: he is not seizing on fields allotted to another, since the Lord constituted him the minister of all the Gentiles.
8:
Where the first of the eighth verse points nobody agrees. Barnes takes it as first not in importance but in order, before the main design; Calvin cites Stuart to the same effect, and reports his suggestion that the particle finds its answering clause only at the thirteenth verse. Robertson observes that the balancing adverb never comes at all: the rush of thoughts crowds out the balanced phraseology. Clarke marks all down to the seventeenth verse as preface, in which the apostle conciliates the Christians at Rome and prepares their minds for his reproofs. Wesley finds in the entrance of the epistle the traces of all spiritual affections, and says my God expresses faith, hope, love, and consequently all true religion. Chrysostom calls the opening an exordium worthy of this blessed spirit, teaching all men to render thanks not for their own well-doings only but for others'; when our affairs are borne onward with a fair wind, he adds, thankfulness is no matter of wonder, but when the vessel veers about and is in jeopardy, then is the great time.

Throughout the whole world the grammarians all soften. Ellicott calls it hyperbole, the more natural since the Apostle speaks of Rome, the metropolis of the world as he knew it; Robertson agrees, though the report spread widely because the church stood in the central city of the empire; Barnes limits world, as Scripture often does, to the parts of the empire where the church stood. Henry gives the report a history: the Roman Christians, scattered through the empire by Claudius's edict banishing the Jews, had now returned and left a good report wherever they went, so that if they had not been persecuted they had not been famous. Calvin restricts it not geographically but by the witnesses: only the faithful proclaimed this faith, since the unbelieving, who deemed it detestable, could give no correct testimony; that the handful were unknown to the ungodly at Rome he counts nothing. Theodoret recites both verses whole.

That the ninth verse contains an oath Gill, Henry and Calvin agree. Gill notes that the appeal is not to any creature in heaven or earth but to God, who alone is to be sworn by; Henry that it is a solemn appeal to the searcher of hearts, in a matter known only to God and his own heart. Calvin makes it a controversy: most foolish is it to deny that the Apostle used an oath here, nor did he thereby transgress Christ's prohibition, for it was not Christ's design, as the superstitious Anabaptists dream, to abolish oaths altogether, but to enforce the law, which allows an oath and condemns only perjury and needless swearing. In solemn oaths, he points out, no one swore by heaven or the throne or the earth or Jerusalem or the head; those were conversational forms, and those alone the Saviour condemned.

Serve is a word of worship. Ellicott says it is used strictly of voluntary service paid to God, especially by sacrifice, and here metaphorically, service rendered with the ritual of the spirit; spirit being with Paul the highest faculty in man, the organ by which he communicates with God, of itself neutral, and apt apart from God's Spirit to fall under the flesh. He quotes Bacon: man is of kin to the beasts by his body, and if he be not of kin to God by his spirit he is a base and ignoble creature. Clarke hears a polemic, the spiritual worship of the Gospel against the external or carnal worship of the Jews: mine is not a religion of ceremonies. Robertson goes to the root instead, an old verb from a word meaning hire, so to serve for wages and then at large. Of the unceasing prayer he remarks that Paul uses both adverbs of the Thessalonians too: he seems to have had prayer lists, never omitting the Romans.
10:
What the spiritual gift is they cannot settle. Clarke takes it of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, conferred only through apostles, so that the Roman Christians, never yet visited by one, differed widely from every other church of Paul's raising. Barnes calls that interpretation forced and unnatural, and denies there is any instance where the expression denotes the power of working miracles. Calvin reports Chalmers and Haldane on Clarke's side and most commentators against them, and settles for any gift or benefit, whether miraculous or ordinary, which the Apostle might be the means of conveying. Ellicott dissolves the question: all the apostolic gifts, miraculous and non-miraculous, are included, and we may believe the Apostle would hardly draw the distinction that we do, both alike being the direct gift of the Spirit.

From the same clause two of them settle the question of Peter's presence at Rome, opposite ways. Wesley infers that St Peter had no more been there than St Paul when the epistle was written, since otherwise what Paul wishes to impart would have been imparted already. Theodoret had reasoned from the same words the other way: because the great Peter had already conveyed to them the doctrines of the gospel, Paul necessarily adds, to the end ye may be established, desiring not to bring another doctrine but to water trees already planted. The twelfth verse all of them read as a correction. Robertson, citing Denney, calls it an explanatory correction and insists the particle should not be ignored. Ellicott makes it a beautiful touch of true courtesy: Paul hastily draws back, unwilling to imply that it is for him only to impart and for them to receive. Wesley says he not only associates the Romans with himself but prefers them before himself, and asks how different this style is from that of the modern court of Rome.

Gill notes what Paul did not long to see at Rome: not the city, which was one of Austin's three wishes, nor the emperor, nor the senate, nor the fine buildings, but the poor saints there. The compound verb defeats them. Calvin prefers Bucer's encouragement to comfort, and stacks up the renderings: Piscator that I may receive consolation, Castelio that we may be together refreshed, Beza in order to receive common exhortation, Schleusner that I may receive joy and pleasure from you, or that by mutual comfort we may console and strengthen one another. Stuart confesses that he has rendered it as he has only because he cannot find any English word which will convey the full sense of the original; Hodge says which sense is to be preferred it is not easy to decide, and settles for a wide one. Ellicott finds in it rather more of our encouraged than of comfort, and refers it to the word translated comforter in John.

Why he had been hindered Ellicott declines to consider: it is hardly worth while to speculate, as some commentators have done, for in a life like his there may have been many causes. The others speculate. Clarke, noting that let is Anglo-Saxon for hinder, thinks the original word points to a divine prohibition, God not seeing right to permit him; Wesley offers business, or persecution, or the Spirit; Calvin says the Lord employed him in more urgent concerns he could not have neglected without loss to the Church, and frequently upsets the purposes of his saints to humble them. Barnes takes the purpose recorded here and in Acts as one of Paley's undesigned coincidences, a contrivance no forger would have thought of; and he observes that the prayer was granted in a remarkable way, Paul reaching Rome in chains after appealing to the emperor. Clarke puts it more bluntly: that he had a prosperous meeting with them we cannot doubt, but that he had a disastrous journey to them the twenty-seventh of the Acts fully proves.
14:
Greeks and Barbarians is a division Paul takes from the Greeks, who, as Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott note, called everyone but themselves barbarians; Robertson adds that the Jews fell on the barbarian side. Where the Romans fall is the question. Barnes puts them among the Greeks, since Paul could not be supposed to call them barbarians, and cites Dionysius of Halicarnassus for their Greek descent; Wesley says the same flatly; Robertson answers obliquely, that they had absorbed the Greek language and culture. Ellicott refuses either class: Paul means all mankind, and, writing from Greece, adopts the Greek point of view. Calvin warns that the second pair does not map onto the first, many unlearned being among the Greeks too.

Calvin draws a double lesson from a debt owed to wise and unwise alike. The gospel is by a heavenly mandate offered to the wise, that every science and the loftiness of all arts may give way to the simplicity of his doctrine, and the learned be made meek enough to bear as fellow-disciples those they would not have deigned to take as scholars; the unlearned are not to be driven from this school, nor to flee it through groundless fear. All teachers have here a rule, to accommodate themselves modestly to the capacities of the ignorant, though they are not so indebted to the foolish as to cherish their folly. Ellicott makes the point historically: the gospel was at first most readily received by the poor and unlearned, but culture was not excluded, and the Church that began with Ignatius and Polycarp numbered before that century closed Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria and Origen, the most learned man of the age.

Of being ashamed each finds a different edge. Gill turns it into a catalogue of those who are: who hide the Gospel having abilities to preach it, who preach it only in part, who own in private what they will not preach in public, who blend it with their inventions and live on applause. Henry lists what might tempt a man to be ashamed of it: its author was hanged upon a tree, its doctrine had little to set it off among scholars, its professors were everywhere spoken against. He reckons him a Christian indeed who is neither ashamed of the gospel nor a shame to it. Clarke reads the word through Isaiah's promise that whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed, that is, not confounded nor disappointed of his hope, and finds the Jews, trusting elsewhere, ashamed of their confidence from that day to this. Ellicott recalls that Paul once found a stumbling-block in the humiliation of the Cross, and that it is now just what he is proudest of.

The power of God Robertson glosses from experience: he had seen the dynamite of God at work; Ellicott calls it the lever by which God would move the world; Calvin insists Paul speaks of no secret revelation but of vocal preaching, so that those who withdraw from hearing the word drive away God's hand. Cyril of Jerusalem argues it from the devils: many have been crucified throughout the world, but by none of these are the devils scared, and at the Sign of this Cross they shudder. Theodoret makes the division of labour plain: it is Paul's to preach, but the believing depends on the hearers. Barnes presses unto salvation further, that one who believed and then fell away could in no correct sense be called saved, so that the apostle opens with the final preservation of the saints; Wesley keeps the condition in view, calling it the means of saving all who accept salvation God's own way. Of to the Jew first Barnes says only that it is first in order of time; Clarke that they had the greatest need as well as the first offer, being more culpable than Gentiles who never had a revelation.
17:
What the righteousness of God means Barnes calls the most important expression in the epistle, and reduces to three possibilities, rejecting two: it is not the attribute of justice displayed, since the leading design of the gospel is not to evince God's justice but his love; nor is it his goodness, which would be a departure from the established meaning of the word. It is God's plan of justifying men, set against man's plan of justifying himself by works. Clarke says the same in fewer words, God's method of saving sinners, proved by collating the ninth and tenth chapters. Ellicott denies the attribute too: of God here means proceeding from God, and names the condition of righteousness into which a man enters by his participation in the Messianic kingdom. Calvin takes it as that which is approved before God's tribunal. Robertson calls it a God kind of righteousness, a subjective genitive carrying two ideas at once, the righteousness God has and the righteousness he bestows.

On what that leaves the believer possessing they divide sharply. Gill says the Father approves and accepts the righteousness Christ wrought by obeying the precepts and bearing the penalty of the law, and imputes it to his elect. Ellicott agrees that such persons are treated as if righteous, the righteousness attributed to them being no merit of their own but an ideal condition in which God places them. Barnes denies the transfer in terms: it is not that his righteousness becomes ours, this is not true, and there is no intelligible sense in which it can be understood; God's plan is to treat us as if we had not sinned, on the ground of what Christ has done in our stead. Robertson widens the word to cover sanctification as well as justification, where Calvin, weighing the same suggestion, holds that this righteousness consists in the free remission of sins and does not include the grace of regeneration.

From faith to faith divides them again. Clarke reads it historically, the faith of the old covenant leading on to the faith of the new, since Abraham was justified before the law was given. Calvin calls that comparison more refined than well-founded, and takes the phrase of each believer's daily progress: when we first taste the gospel we see God's smiling countenance turned towards us, but at a distance, and as knowledge grows we behold his favour more clearly and familiarly. Ellicott says much the same, that the gospel confirms and strengthens the very faculty by which it was apprehended. Wesley makes it a gradual series of still clearer promises. Barnes rejects the whole class of readings with five objections, chief among them that the gospel never supposed men to have a degree of faith by nature needing only to be strengthened, and attaches the words instead to the righteousness itself. Theodoret notes only that it is not revealed to all, but to those who have the eyes of faith.

Habakkuk they handle with care. Clarke reports two pointings of the Greek and prefers the second, not the just shall live by faith but the just by faith shall live, that is, he alone who is justified by faith shall be saved. Ellicott inclines the same way. Barnes insists the prophet did not refer originally to justification at all, but to the Babylonish captivity, and that those who trusted God should be restored and preserved; Wesley agrees that it was primarily spoken of those who saved their lives when the Chaldeans besieged Jerusalem. Calvin observes that Paul quotes the words exactly from neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint, dropping the pronoun both carry, his object being to state the general truth of the passage rather than to quote it verbally. Clarke also derives our word from the Anglo-Saxon rightwiseness, from right and to know, so that the righteous man is he that knows most and acts best.
18:
Chrysostom notes the turn: after the gentler things Paul goes over to the more fearful, because most men are drawn less by the promise of good than by the fear of pain, and God accordingly did not only promise a kingdom but also threaten hell. What the wrath is, the rest hasten to qualify. Barnes says the word properly denotes the desire of a man injured and enraged, and is thus synonymous with revenge, but applied to God it must be divested of every human passion, since he cannot be injured and has no motive for vengeance; the nature of a feeling is judged by the person's character, as when the Saviour looked on his disciples with the same word. Calvin goes further: the term imports no emotion in God at all, but refers only to the perception of the sinner who is punished. Robertson traces it to a verb meaning to teem or swell, and takes it with Shedd as the wrath not of rage but of reason and law.

From heaven Barnes takes to mean only that the displeasure is made known by an arrangement showing its origin in heaven, rejecting the readings that the heavens declare it and that Christ the executioner will be manifest from heaven. Calvin refuses the adjectival sense, the wrath of the celestial God, for something more emphatic: wheresoever a man looks he will find no salvation, for the wrath of God is poured out on the whole world to the full extent of heaven. Where the revelation is to be read they differ: Ellicott infers it from the actual condition, the degradation doubly degraded, in which sin leaves its votaries; Calvin records that Stuart, Macknight and Pareus referred the wrath, no less than the righteousness, to the gospel itself, as Haldane would not.

Whether ungodliness and unrighteousness are two faults or one divides them cleanly. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson keep them apart, the first naming offences against God and the second against men, and Henry maps them onto the two tables of the law. Calvin knows the distinction and refuses it: since the Apostle refers this unrighteousness to the neglect of true religion, both words designate one thing, ingratitude towards God, impiety as it dishonours him and unrighteousness because man, transferring to himself what belongs to God, robs him of his glory. Holding the truth nearly all of them read as hindering it, Wesley noting that the truth struggles against their wickedness. Clarke reports Rosenmuller's contention that the verb means not to hold but to hinder, and the suggestion that the clause fits their best philosophers, Socrates, Plato and Seneca, who knew more of the Divine nature than they thought prudent to discover. Robertson puts it plainly: the truth is out in the open, but wicked men put it in a box and sit on the lid.

Robertson calls what may be known of God a verbal adjective meaning either the known or the knowable; Ellicott takes it as what is generally known, the truths of so-called natural religion. Gill lists what the light of nature could not reach: a trinity of persons in the Godhead, the incarnation of the Mediator, the resurrection of the dead, and the manner of worshipping God with acceptance. Barnes grants that the mass of the heathen world was ignorant of the true God, locating the knowledge with their philosophers, and holds only that they knew enough to be inexcusable. Calvin sets the same limit: God accommodates to our small capacities what he testifies of himself, so that insane are all they who seek to know of themselves what God is. Where it is manifest they part: Ellicott says imprinted on their consciences and calls the marginal to them hardly tenable; Calvin reports Stuart taking it of the visible world, before their eyes. Theodoret says only that nature taught them, and asks who gave the knowledge.
20:
Gill says what the invisible things are not: not the angels, nor the unseen glories of another world, nor the decrees of God, nor the persons in the Godhead, but his perfections, which the verse itself explains as his eternal power and Godhead. Theodoret makes something of the plural, that Paul says not the invisible thing but invisible things: his creation, his providence, his just sentence on each person, and all his dispensations. Ellicott hears a play on words, the unseen seen, discerned by the eye of the mind; Wesley says the same, adding that they are seen by them only who use their understanding. From the creation of the world Barnes takes instrumentally rather than historically, by means of the universe rather than ever since the act of creating, the design being not to state a fact of history but to show the means of knowledge within reach; Robertson keeps the temporal sense.

On Godhead they are precise. Robertson notes that Paul uses one word here and another at Colossians, and gives Sanday and Headlam's distinction, the one Divine Personality, the other Divine Nature and properties. Ellicott says the same in his own terms, that divinity would perhaps be a more correct translation, since what is meant is divine nature rather than divine personality, a name a pagan philosopher might have used as readily as a Christian. Calvin's editor adds that the word carries besides the idea of goodness, since the next verse charges two things answering to the two here, that they neither glorified him nor were thankful; and he cites Venema that many heathen made goodness the primary attribute of Deity.

Calvin sets out what a right notion of God includes: eternity, because he is the maker of all things; power, because he holds all things in his hand; wisdom, because he has arranged them in so exquisite an order; goodness, since there is no other cause than himself why he created them; justice, because he punishes the guilty and defends the innocent; mercy, because he bears with so much forbearance the perversity of men; truth, because he is unchangeable. Then he qualifies it: the manifestation is, as regards the light itself, sufficiently clear, and on account of our blindness not sufficient. We conceive that there is a Deity, and conclude that whoever he may be he ought to be worshipped, but our reason fails, because it cannot ascertain who or what sort of being God is; so that this knowledge, which avails only to take away excuse, differs greatly from that which brings salvation. Barnes turns the argument forward: the proof was clear even to the heathen with their imperfect astronomy, and is grander under the full blaze of modern science, so that those in Christian lands who know the discoveries and do not reflect have no shadow of excuse.

That the philosophers knew better than they taught both Barnes and Clarke maintain, citing Warburton. Barnes adds Cudworth and Cicero, and repeats Gibbon's summary that the philosophers held all the popular superstitions equally false, the common people equally true, and the politicians equally useful. Clarke presses it into an indictment: they did not proclaim him to the people but shut up his glory in their mysteries, giving them in exchange an image made like to corruptible man; and God in punishment suffered those mysteries, erected for a school of virtue, to degenerate into an odious sink of vice. Of what the reasonings produced, Calvin's editor preserves Pareus's catalogue, from Epicurus who denied and Protagoras who doubted, through the dispute whether the gods were corporeal, down to the Egyptians who worshipped oxen and crocodiles and what grew in their gardens, garlic and onions; and Wesley points to Lucretius. The foolish heart Robertson glosses as the unintelligent one, not able to put together the manifest evidence; Barnes reminds us that the Hebrews said heart where we say head.
22:
Who is meant by those professing wisdom is Calvin's one open quarrel with the rest, and his own editor marks him the odd man out. Gill, Barnes and Clarke take it of the philosophers, Gill noting that the learned first called themselves wise men and afterwards, to cover their pride, lovers of wisdom. Calvin denies the restriction: it was not peculiar to the philosophers to suppose themselves wise in the knowledge of God, but common to all nations and ranks, a presumption not learned in the schools but innate, coming with us from the womb; the error of image-making did not originate with them, who merely approved what they received from others. His editor sets against this Beza's roll of the reputed learned in every nation, the Druids of the Gauls, the soothsayers of the Tuscans, the priests of the Egyptians, the magi of the Persians, the gymnosophists of the Indians and the Rabbins of the Jews. Ellicott presses the passive: they were made fools, the folly judicially inflicted as punishment for the first step of declension; Robertson calls the phrase an oxymoron that cuts to the bone.

Whether the worshipper took the image for the god Calvin will not allow as a defence: they are not excused by the pretence that they believed God dwells in heaven and counted not the wood to be God but his image, since it is a high indignity to form so gross an idea of his majesty as to dare to make an image of him at all; and none were exempt, neither priests nor statesmen nor philosophers, even Plato having sought some likeness of God. Ellicott allows the distinction to few: the images in Greece and the beasts in Egypt were by some regarded only as symbols of the Deity, but probably only a small minority could draw it. Calvin also prefers corruptible man to Erasmus's mortal man: Paul sets not the immortality of God against man's mortality, but that glory which is subject to no defects against man's most wretched condition.

What was worshipped they catalogue with relish. Barnes explains the ibis by the serpents it destroyed, and adds the hawk in Egypt, the eagle at Rome, the ox called apis after which Israel made its calf, the dog and the monkey; he notes a second-century sect, the Ophites, who worshipped a serpent and claimed to be Christians, and that even the leek and the onion had worshippers. Ellicott quotes a longer list: cats and weasels and otters, the hoopoe and stork, the sheep worshipped in Sais and eaten in Lycopolis, the crocodile sacred in most of the land but chased and eaten in Tentyra, and the sacred serpent fed with veal fat in holes in all the temples. Theodoret puts the sting in it: some of these creatures men eat as food, some loathe as unclean, some avoid as noxious, and these very things they made gods.

What God gave them up means divides them again. Theodoret says plainly that Paul puts gave them up for permitted, God depriving them of his special providence and letting them drift like an unsteady vessel; Barnes denies any positive influence, Wesley makes it the withdrawing of restraining grace, Clarke a permitting them to plunge. Calvin refuses the softening: they wrest the word who think we are led into sin only by God's permission, for as Satan is the minister of God's wrath and as it were the executioner, he is armed against us not through the connivance but by the command of his judge; and Calvin's editor quotes Augustine going further, that God delivered them up not only by sufferance but by power and as it were by an efficient operation. On the threefold repetition Wesley finds three degrees of ungodliness and of punishment, where Robertson finds not three stages but one withdrawal repeated, the words sounding like clods on the coffin.
25:
The truth of God into a lie both Barnes and Calvin read as a Hebraism: one of two nouns serves as an adjective, so that the phrase means the true God, and a lie means an idol. Gill guards it: the truth meant is not the Gospel, with which they were unacquainted. Ellicott takes the preposition instrumentally, literally with a lie, the lie being the instrument by which the substitution was made; Robertson counts the exchange as a trade, and quotes Bengel calling it the price of mythology. On worshipping the creature more than the Creator Calvin's editor collects four renderings and prefers the last two: Erasmus above the Creator, Luther rather than the Creator, Beza to the neglect of the Creator, Grotius in the place of the Creator, since those described did not worship God at all, the preposition elsewhere marking exclusion. Robertson keeps the comparison: set side by side, they preferred the creature.

The doxology they all pause over. Ellicott ascribes it to an impulse of reverential feeling, the Apostle being shocked at the language he finds himself using and the connection in which the most Holy Name has been mentioned; Robertson calls it one of the doxologies that may come at any moment when Paul is greatly stirred; Barnes notes the Jewish custom of adding an ascription of praise whenever the name was spoken, and recalls that Robert Boyle never mentioned the name of God without a solemn pause. Theodoret alone turns the verse into a doctrinal argument: to the same reproach lie open those who call the only-begotten Son a creature and yet worship him as God, since they ought either, admitting his divinity, to rank him with God who begat him, or, pronouncing him created, not to adore him as divine.

How far to document the charge divides Barnes from Clarke. Barnes first defends the making of it, that the shame lies not in specifying these things but in their existence, not in the apostle but in those who practised them, and that no man would venture such charges without evidence, since the accused could simply have denied them; he then fills a page with citations from Maximus Tyrius, Cicero, Xenophon, Plato, Aristotle, Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius and Seneca, adding a modern traveller's report of China. Clarke declines the labour: he could produce a multitude of proofs from their own writings, but it is needless to make the subject plainer than the apostle has left it. He offers a cause instead, that their idolatry necessarily produced such impurity, since the highest objects of their worship were themselves represented as adulterers; and Wesley observes that the heathen Romans were then abandoned to this to the last degree, and none more than the emperors.

Chrysostom argues from the words changed and leaving that no excuse remains: none can say they were hindered of what was lawful, for changing implies possession; and since what is contrary to nature carries an irksomeness with it, they cannot fairly allege even pleasure, genuine pleasure being according to nature. What the recompense received in themselves is they divide over. Ellicott makes the error the turning from God to idols and the recompense the excesses themselves; Theodoret says infamy is the severest penalty of such affections, and that they voluntarily brought on themselves what not even a victorious enemy had attempted; Wesley makes the idolatry punished by the lust. Barnes and Clarke take it bodily, of enervated frames, barrenness and premature decay, while Robertson says only that the debt will be paid in full, nature attending to it in their own bodies and souls. Gill names the sin from Sodom; Calvin answers the objection that no one man was laden with the whole mass of vices, since in arraigning the common baseness of men it is proof enough that all acknowledge some fault; and Henry turns the chapter into a call to self-examination.
28:
They all hear the pun. Ellicott states it flatly: as they reprobated the knowledge of God so he gave them up to a reprobate mind, and as they would have nothing to do with him, so he would have nothing to do with them; reprobate meaning properly tried and found wanting, and so cast away as worthless. Robertson takes the verb from the assaying of coins: they tested God and turned aside from him, and God rejected their mental attitude in turn. Clarke keeps the echo, rendering the first verb they did not search and the noun an unsearching or undiscerning mind, since it is the same word in both places. Calvin's editor is satisfied with no English attempt, surveying Beza's mind void of all judgment, Locke's unsearching mind, Macknight's unapproving mind and Doddridge's undiscerning mind, allowing the last nearest, and settling for an unattesting mind, not capable of bringing things to the test. Ellicott adds that even as here means not because but in like proportion as, the punishment answering exactly to the degree of the deflection.

Chrysostom presses the same clause for a different purpose. Paul did not write as they knew not God, he observes, but as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, which shows the sin to have been one of a perverted determination of obstinacy rather than of a sudden ravishment; and further that it was not the flesh, as some heretics say, but the mind whose wicked lust the sins belonged to, since when he is corrupted who held the reins all else is dragged out of course. Theodoret says it more briefly: had they been willing to know him they would have followed the divine laws. Whom the catalogue describes Gill restricts sharply: Paul is speaking not of the common people but of their wise professors and moral instructors, who under the guise of morality were guilty of the greatest pride. Calvin takes it the other way: having cited one abomination not common to all, Paul begins here to enumerate vices from which none was free.

The first two names in the list they gloss in opposite directions. Calvin, citing Ammonius, makes wickedness the practised doing of mischief and maliciousness the depravity of mind that harms a neighbour, and Ellicott agrees, the latter being the disposition and the former its active exercise. Barnes reverses the pair, making wickedness the desire of injuring others and the other word the act rather than the desire, and cites Calvin for the gloss. Of fornication, which stands third in the received text and which Barnes, Clarke, Wesley and Theodoret all expound, Ellicott says it is wanting in the best manuscripts and should be omitted, as should implacable three verses later; Robertson calls it not genuine here. Robertson notices what the printed list conceals, that no connective appears anywhere in these verses, for dramatic effect, and that envy and murder are paired as like-sounding words.

On murder Barnes turns to the amphitheatre, where Nero at one show exhibited four hundred senators and six hundred knights as gladiators, and where, on Gibbon's reckoning, several thousand victims might be slaughtered annually; he tells how under Probus seven hundred gladiators, disdaining to shed their blood for the amusement of the populace, killed their keepers and filled the streets of Rome with blood, and notes that the shows lasted until the first Christian emperor abolished them. Clarke answers with poetry, printing Ovid's personification of Envy in Addison's translation: she never smiles but when the wretched weep, and bears her own tormentor in her breast. Of debate Barnes warns that the English word now means discussion for eliciting truth, as in Congress, where the original meant heated strife; Ellicott adds that it is not specially verbal contention. Whisperers Barnes distinguishes from open calumniators as more dangerous, hinting at evil under an injunction of secrecy, knowing it will be divulged.
30:
One word in the list splits them. Barnes takes haters of God at full strength, the highest possible crime, no creed giving a more humiliating representation of human wickedness; Clarke glosses it atheists and contemners of sacred things, Wesley deniers of providence, and Calvin says there is no reason for a passive sense, since Paul is here proving men guilty by manifest vices. Ellicott answers that it should rather be hated by God, since there seem to be no examples of the active sense, and Robertson agrees that all the ancient examples are passive, the Vulgate reading it so. The three words that follow Ellicott arranges as act, thought and word: insolence in outward bearing, self-esteem mixed with contempt, and braggadocio in language. Calvin's editor makes the same three properties of a proud spirit.

Inventors of evil things they read four ways. Barnes takes it of new forms of luxury and vice, since the passions cease to be gratified by the old, and points to the games and theatres of Rome. Clarke takes it of invented religious observances, the orgies of Bacchus, the mysteries of Ceres and the lupercalia. Robertson takes it of new forms of vice such as Nero devised. Wesley spreads it widest: new pleasures, new ways of gain, and new arts of hurting, particularly in war. On whisperers and backbiters Barnes and Calvin agree in a distinction, the first working by secret accusation while the second proclaim publicly and spare no one's reputation; Robertson will not have it, calling the second word talkers back whether secretly or openly, and noting that the first is onomatopoetic.

Without natural affection Barnes documents at length, since the attachment of parents to children is among the strongest in nature and only confirmed wickedness can overcome it. He collects the Spartan law throwing weak or deformed infants into the cavern at Taygetus, Aristotle enjoining exposure of the feeble to check population, the rule of Romulus that only male children and the eldest daughter be reared, Pliny defending the right, and Tertullian charging the Romans with drowning, starving and exposing their children to dogs, the practice ending only under the first Christian emperor. Wesley adds the killing of the aged and helpless; Ellicott notes that infanticide and divorce were both common then. Of covenant-breakers Wesley says the Romans as a nation never scrupled to vacate a solemn engagement they disliked, giving up the general who made it and supposing themselves at liberty; Robertson calls them men who treat covenants as a scrap of paper, and adds that implacable, which Clarke derives from the libation poured at a treaty, is carried into this verse from elsewhere.

The last clause they take for the worst. Calvin says the Apostle meant to condemn something more grievous than the vices themselves, the patronage of vice against the righteousness of God, for it is the summit of all evils when the sinner is so void of shame that he is pleased with his own vices and cherishes them in others; he who is ashamed is as yet healable, but when such impudence is contracted by habit there is no more hope of reformation. Wesley says a man may be hurried by his passions to do the thing he hates, but he that has pleasure in those who do evil loves wickedness for its own sake; Ellicott says the approval is given in cold blood, a perversion of conscience rather than a momentary yielding; Theodoret calls it the last excess, since they ought to loathe even their own transgressions. Barnes observes that men seldom sin alone but join hand in hand, and closes with Livy, that Rome had so increased by her virtues that she could bear neither her vices nor their remedy, and with Seneca, that innocence had ceased to exist. Gill takes the judgment known to be the law and light of nature.
